text: Antonio still takes his orders from ETA and no longer believes a word of the cause that issues them. Days remain before the attack. Imanol Uribe refuses to let that countdown behave like one: Antonio meets Charo, who is young, using, and living in conditions that have not yet reached her. Ninety-three minutes is tight for a thriller carrying this much political weight, and the compression does the argument's work, since there is no room for debate scenes and the disagreement has to happen inside a man whose hands are supposed to stay steady. It took the Goya for Best Film. What holds is not the plan but the waiting: rented rooms, a city going about its business, and a gunman obliged to keep pretending the days are ordinary.

The escape route runs the wrong way, out of Mexico City and back to Madrid, where what waits is domestic. Gloria drinks, works the street, and comes home to a husband who cannot answer her and a mother-in-law who can. Agustín Díaz Yanes builds the pursuit as slow arithmetic: the hitman Eduardo wants what she knows, and she has almost nothing else left to trade. The Goyas took the film's measure through its people, with Best Actress, Best Actor and Best Editing alongside Best Film, and that distribution is accurate, because performance and rhythm are where the pressure sits. Nothing in the first hour is styled up. Two women in a small flat, one of them working out what a piece of information might be worth to the men who want it.

The outboard motor is stolen, and with it goes the only scheduled contact a lakeside village has with anywhere else. Andrei Konchalovsky cast the villagers as themselves and spent more than a year finding the man who would carry the mail, and the search shows in how little anyone performs. A spaceport operates nearby. So do phones and televisions. None of it has produced work, government or services here, and the film lets that contradiction sit in the frame instead of arguing about it. Ninety minutes, mostly water and weather and the way people talk when the same faces have been around for decades. Venice gave the direction its Silver Lion. The harder thing it does is treat a routine that means nothing to the mainland as the structure holding a handful of lives upright.

Everything turns on an object: a sword the clans want, and a new order of fighters formed to keep it from the wrong hands. Ron Yuan directs 106 minutes of American fantasy built on Japanese material, in English, working from the genre's old promise that a blade can settle a question of legitimacy. The premise is familiar and the film proceeds as if that were settled, which pushes the interest toward staging rather than story: how a company of warriors gets assembled, what a duel looks like once magic is on the table, how much weight choreography can carry when the outcome is never seriously in doubt. Reception has been cool. Taken as craft, it is doing an unglamorous and quite specific job at feature length, with close attention to where bodies actually go.

A diagnosis does what years of estrangement had prevented: it puts the two brothers in the same room. Patrice Chéreau keeps the film to ninety-two minutes and largely inside hospital time, with its waiting, its procedures, its small indignities of being handled. The estrangement had a cause, one brother's refusal to accept the other's sexuality, and the reunion does not dissolve that so much as postpone it. Meanwhile both men's partners find themselves outside a closeness they cannot enter, which is the film's least sentimental idea: intimacy restored between two people registers as a loss to everyone standing nearby. Berlin recognized the direction with a Silver Bear, and the lead performance took a European Film Award. The camera stays close to skin, and the body turns out to be the subject, the plot only its schedule.

Two men grew up together, and one of them has just married a young woman the other cannot stop looking at. Carlos Saura makes Julián a provincial doctor, single, middle-aged, careful with everything he can control, and then puts Elena in his consulting room as his oldest friend's wife. Over ninety minutes the film behaves less like melodrama than like a case file: attention hardening into appetite, appetite becoming a project with stages. Saura's subject is the method, a man with clinical habits applying them to another person, adjusting, comparing, correcting a resemblance. Berlin awarded the direction a Silver Bear. The unsettling part is not the desire, which declares itself early, but the tidiness, since almost everything Julián does would read as reasonable written up in a chart.

The forest is in Galicia and it is crowded, with travelers worth robbing and with everyone else who has business among the trees. Malvís is not much of a bandit. He is a day laborer who ran out of patience with day labor and decided highway robbery was a trade a man could learn, and José Luis Cuerda plays that for comedy without once making him ridiculous. The film moves in episodes rather than plot, one encounter handing off to the next, and across 108 minutes the effect is of a place being surveyed by its own inhabitants: the fear of the woods and the gossip of the woods turn out to be a single conversation. It took the Goya for Best Film. Comedy of this kind depends on knowing exactly how poor everybody is, and Cuerda keeps that figure in view throughout.

A prison in Valencia holds a ceremony to honor the men it once locked up. The occasion is official: political prisoners of the Franco years, recognized at last, with speeches and dignitaries and photographers arranged inside the walls. Luis García Berlanga then fills the room past its capacity. The crowd swells, the protocol slips, and the event starts running on its own momentum while the organizers chase after it. Ninety-nine minutes, largely one occasion, and the comedy is architectural, made of corridors and doorways and a courtyard where everyone talks at once and nobody is quite in charge. It won the Goya for Best Film. The edge is easy to miss: a country commemorating its own repression finds that the ceremony is also a reunion, and reunions are hard to keep respectable.

Five chapters, two households, 135 minutes, and the structure is announced early and then honored without a flourish. Adela moves to Madrid with her baby after a separation. Antonia keeps a shop and has three grown daughters with three sets of demands. Jaime Rosales films them at the pitch of ordinary maintenance: rent, shifts, an illness, who owes whom money and who is willing to say so. In place of a crisis engine there is the accumulating cost of arrangements that were supposed to be temporary. The Goya for Best Film went to it, which is unusual for something this withholding. What the length buys is a shift in attention, so that after an hour a conversation about a flat lands with the weight plot ordinarily carries.

A Spanish production, shot in English, set in Paris, about an American who writes screenplays he does not respect. Fernando Trueba puts his writer to work for a young director whose talent is not the problem and whose company is intolerable, then introduces the director's sister, cold in a way that reads as an invitation. From there the film works less as mystery than as a study in professional humiliation: a man selling his craft in a language and a city not his own, telling himself the arrangement is temporary. Its 108 minutes take their time with the drift, which is where the interest lies, the small compromises being far more persuasive than the machinery built around them. The Goya for Best Film went to it. Trueba's real subject is vanity, and how efficiently other people use it once they have found it.

Semetka's unit is looking for partisans, and the looking is most of what this war consists of. A Hungarian farmer carrying a sub-lieutenant's rank moves through occupied Soviet territory in weather that makes every field the same field, and then the commander is killed and command falls to him. Dénes Nagy keeps the camera down among the men, and across 103 minutes the result is a war film with very little combat and a great deal of cold, mud and waiting, which is where ordinary men become answerable for things they never chose. Berlin recognized the direction with a Silver Bear, and the production design took a European Film Award. The pressure is not whether Semetka can fight. It is whether he can hold a unit together in a country where every village is a question with no safe answer.

A woman arrives on an island to collect votes, accompanied by a soldier with a rifle. Neither of them chose the other. Babak Payami sends the pair out to find islanders who may or may not hold opinions about a national ballot, and the comedy sits in the gap between a procedure and the place it has been dropped into. The soldier trusts the rules he was trained on. The agent works from a different set, and their disagreements do most of the work a plot would usually do, across 105 minutes paced like an errand nobody can hurry. Venice awarded the direction a Silver Lion. The straight face is the whole technique, since no one on screen treats the vote as absurd, and that seriousness is what makes the day funny and then, gradually, something other than funny.

A thirteen-year-old is missing for a week, then walks back in as though the week had been an errand. Angela Schanelec starts after the return rather than during the absence, and that reordering changes everything, since the mother and the teachers are left holding a question with no procedure attached to it. The film offers them no reassurance and the audience less. Scenes arrive without connective tissue and are held long past the point where they would ordinarily be cut, and the speech is flat enough that the usual hierarchy between a line and a gesture stops applying. Berlin gave the direction a Silver Bear. The difficulty is deliberate, and it is not withheld information: it is a refusal to convert fear into shapes that would make it easy to recognize.

Factory in the morning, family in the evening, and the Rhône moving past all of it without comment. Vincent has done this long enough that the pattern no longer requires him to be awake for it. Then his father hands him money and he goes, not dramatically, not with a speech, simply away for a while. Otar Ioseliani spends 126 minutes on a story that could be told in forty, because the texture of the days matters more here than the shape of the decision: gestures repeated until they turn comic, dialogue treated as one sound among others, long stretches that play as observed behavior rather than scenes. Berlin gave the direction a Silver Bear. Nothing is underlined, and the humor comes from how much of a routine a man carries with him when he leaves one.
